(i) This Question Paper contains 38 questions. All questions are compulsory.
(ii) Question paper is divided into five Sections – Section A, B, C, D and E.
(iii) In Section A – Questions no. 1 to 18 are Multiple Choice Questions (MCQ's) and Q.no. 19 & 20 are Assertion-Reason based questions of 1 mark each.
(iv) In Section B – Questions no. 21 to 25 are Very Short Answer (VSA) type questions, carrying 2 marks each.
(v) In Section C – Questions no. 26 to 31 are Short Answer (SA) type questions carrying 3 marks each.
(vi) In Section D – Questions no. 32 to 35 are Long Answer (LA) type questions carrying 5 marks each.
(vii) In Section E – Questions no. 36 to 38 are case study based questions, carrying 4 marks each.
(viii) There is no overall choice. However, an internal choice has been provided in 2 questions in Section B, 3 questions in Section C, 3 questions in Section D and 2 questions in Section E.
(ix) Use of calculators is not allowed.

questions.stem: If $\begin{bmatrix} a & c & 0 \\ b & d & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 5 \end{bmatrix}$ is a scalar matrix, then the value of $a + 2b + 3c + 4d$ is :
questions.solution:
Given $\begin{bmatrix} a & c & 0 \\ b & d & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 5 \end{bmatrix}$ is a scalar matrix.
$\Rightarrow a = d = 5$ and $b = c = 0$
$\therefore a + 2b + 3c + 4d = 5 + (2 \times 0) + (3 \times 0) + (4 \times 5) = 25$

questions.stem: Given that $A^{-1} = \frac{1}{7}\begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ -3 & 2 \end{bmatrix}$, matrix $A$ is :
questions.solution:
Given $A^{-1} = \frac{1}{7}\begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ -3 & 2 \end{bmatrix}$
Also $A^{-1} = \frac{\operatorname{adj}(A)}{|A|}$
$\Rightarrow \operatorname{adj}(A) = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ -3 & 2 \end{bmatrix}$
$\therefore A = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & -1 \\ 3 & 2 \end{bmatrix}$

questions.stem: If $A = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ -4 & -2 \end{bmatrix}$, then the value of $I - A + A^{2} - A^{3} + \ldots$ is :
questions.solution:
Given $A = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ -4 & -2 \end{bmatrix}$
$\Rightarrow A^{2} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ -4 & -2 \end{bmatrix} \cdot \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ -4 & -2 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}$
$\therefore I - A + A^{2} - A^{3} + \ldots = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} - \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ -4 & -2 \end{bmatrix} + \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix} - \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix} + \ldots = \begin{bmatrix} -1 & -1 \\ 4 & 3 \end{bmatrix}$

questions.stem: If $A = \begin{bmatrix} -2 & 0 & 0 \\ 1 & 2 & 3 \\ 5 & 1 & -1 \end{bmatrix}$, then the value of $|A(\operatorname{adj}. A)|$ is :
questions.solution:
Given $A = \begin{bmatrix} -2 & 0 & 0 \\ 1 & 2 & 3 \\ 5 & 1 & -1 \end{bmatrix}$
$\Rightarrow |A(\operatorname{adj}. A)| = |A| \cdot |\operatorname{adj}. A| = |A| \cdot |A|^{3-1}$
$= |A|^{3} = \left[-2(-2-3)\right]^{3} = 1000$

questions.stem: Given that $\begin{bmatrix} 1 & x \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 4 & 0 \\ -2 & 0 \end{bmatrix} = O$, the value of $x$ is :
questions.solution:
Given $\begin{bmatrix} 1 & x \end{bmatrix}_{1 \times 2}\begin{bmatrix} 4 & 0 \\ -2 & 0 \end{bmatrix}_{2 \times 2} = O$
$\Rightarrow \begin{bmatrix} 4-2x & 0 \end{bmatrix}_{1 \times 2} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}$
$\therefore 4 - 2x = 0$ or $x = 2$

questions.stem: Derivative of $e^{2x}$ with respect to $e^{x}$, is :
questions.solution:
Let $e^{2x} = v$ and $e^{x} = w$
$\Rightarrow \frac{dv}{dw} = \frac{dv/dx}{dw/dx} = \frac{2e^{2x}}{e^{x}} = 2e^{x}$

questions.stem:
For what value of $k$, the function given below is continuous at $x = 0$?
$$f(x) = \begin{cases} \dfrac{\sqrt{4+x}-2}{x}, & x \neq 0 \\ k, & x = 0 \end{cases}$$
questions.solution:
Since the given function is continuous at $x = 0$,
$\Rightarrow \lim_{x \to 0} f(x) = f(0)$
$\Rightarrow \lim_{x \to 0} \frac{\sqrt{4+x}-2}{x} = k$
$\Rightarrow \lim_{x \to 0} \frac{(\sqrt{4+x}-2)}{x} \times \frac{(\sqrt{4+x}+2)}{(\sqrt{4+x}+2)} = k$
$\Rightarrow \lim_{x \to 0} \frac{x}{x(\sqrt{4+x}+2)} = k$
$\Rightarrow \lim_{x \to 0} \frac{1}{\sqrt{4+x}+2} = k$
$\Rightarrow k = \frac{1}{4}$

questions.stem: The value of $\int_{0}^{3} \frac{dx}{\sqrt{9-x^{2}}}$ is :
questions.solution: $I = \int_{0}^{3} \frac{dx}{\sqrt{9-x^{2}}} = \left[\sin^{-1}\left(\frac{x}{3}\right)\right]_{0}^{3} = \left[\sin^{-1}(1) - \sin^{-1}(0)\right] = \frac{\pi}{2}$

questions.stem: The general solution of the differential equation $x\,dy + y\,dx = 0$ is :
questions.solution:
Given $x\,dy + y\,dx = 0$
$\Rightarrow x\,dy = -y\,dx \Rightarrow \frac{-dy}{y} = \frac{dx}{x}$
Integrating both sides, we get :
$\int \frac{-dy}{y} = \int \frac{dx}{x}$
$\Rightarrow -\log y = \log x - \log c$
$\Rightarrow xy = c$

questions.stem: The integrating factor of the differential equation $(x + 2y^{2})\frac{dy}{dx} = y$ $(y > 0)$ is :
questions.solution:
Given differential equation is $(x + 2y^{2})\frac{dy}{dx} = y\ (y > 0)$
$\Rightarrow \frac{dx}{dy} = \frac{x + 2y^{2}}{y} \Rightarrow \frac{dx}{dy} + \left(\frac{-1}{y}\right)x = 2y$
Comparing this with $\frac{dx}{dy} + P_{1}x = Q_{1}$, we have :
Integrating factor, I.F. $= e^{\int P_{1}\,dy} = e^{\int \frac{-1}{y}dy} = e^{-\log_{e} y} = \frac{1}{y}$

questions.stem: If $\vec{a}$ and $\vec{b}$ are two vectors such that $|\vec{a}| = 1$, $|\vec{b}| = 2$ and $\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b} = \sqrt{3}$, then the angle between $2\vec{a}$ and $-\vec{b}$ is :
questions.solution:
Let $\theta$ be the angle between $2\vec{a}$ and $(-\vec{b})$
$\Rightarrow \cos\theta = \frac{(2\vec{a}) \cdot (-\vec{b})}{|2\vec{a}|\,|-\vec{b}|} = \frac{-2(\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b})}{2 \times |\vec{a}| \times |-\vec{b}|} = \frac{-2 \times \sqrt{3}}{2 \times 1 \times 2} = \frac{-\sqrt{3}}{2}$
$\Rightarrow \theta = \frac{5\pi}{6} \in [0, \pi]$

questions.stem: The vectors $\vec{a} = 2\hat{i} - \hat{j} + \hat{k}$, $\vec{b} = \hat{i} - 3\hat{j} - 5\hat{k}$ and $\vec{c} = -3\hat{i} + 4\hat{j} + 4\hat{k}$ represent the sides of
questions.solution:
Given vectors are : $\vec{a} = 2\hat{i} - \hat{j} + \hat{k}$, $\vec{b} = \hat{i} - 3\hat{j} - 5\hat{k}$ and $\vec{c} = -3\hat{i} + 4\hat{j} + 4\hat{k}$
Now, $\vec{a} + \vec{b} + \vec{c} = \vec{0}$
Hence, these vectors represent the sides of a triangle.
Also, $|\vec{a}| = \sqrt{6}$, $|\vec{b}| = \sqrt{35}$ and $|\vec{c}| = \sqrt{41}$
$\because |\vec{c}|^{2} = |\vec{a}|^{2} + |\vec{b}|^{2}$
$\Rightarrow$ The given triangle will be a right-angled triangle

questions.stem: Let $\vec{a}$ be any vector such that $|\vec{a}| = a$. The value of $|\vec{a} \times \hat{i}|^{2} + |\vec{a} \times \hat{j}|^{2} + |\vec{a} \times \hat{k}|^{2}$ is :
questions.solution:
Let $\vec{a} = x\hat{i} + y\hat{j} + z\hat{k}$
$\Rightarrow |\vec{a}| = \sqrt{x^{2}+y^{2}+z^{2}} = a$
Now, $\vec{a} \times \hat{i} = \begin{vmatrix} \hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k} \\ x & y & z \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \end{vmatrix} = z\hat{j} - y\hat{k}$
Similarly, $\vec{a} \times \hat{j} = z\hat{i} - x\hat{k}$ and $\vec{a} \times \hat{k} = y\hat{i} - x\hat{j}$
$\Rightarrow |\vec{a} \times \hat{i}|^{2} + |\vec{a} \times \hat{j}|^{2} + |\vec{a} \times \hat{k}|^{2} = (z^{2}+y^{2}) + (z^{2}+x^{2}) + (y^{2}+x^{2}) = 2(x^{2}+y^{2}+z^{2}) = 2a^{2}$

questions.stem: The vector equation of a line passing through the point $(1, -1, 0)$ and parallel to Y-axis is :
questions.solution:
Y-axis has direction ratios as $0, 1, 0$
$\Rightarrow$ Vector equation of a line passing through $(1, -1, 0)$ and parallel to Y-axis is :
$\vec{r} = (\hat{i} - \hat{j} + 0\hat{k}) + \lambda(0\hat{i} + \hat{j} + 0\hat{k}) \Rightarrow \vec{r} = (\hat{i} - \hat{j}) + \lambda(\hat{j})$

questions.stem: The lines $\frac{1-x}{2} = \frac{y-1}{3} = \frac{z}{1}$ and $\frac{2x-3}{2p} = \frac{y}{-1} = \frac{z-4}{7}$ are perpendicular to each other for $p$ equal to:
questions.solution:
Given lines are :
$L_{1} : \frac{1-x}{2} = \frac{y-1}{3} = \frac{z}{1} \Rightarrow \frac{x-1}{-2} = \frac{y-1}{3} = \frac{z}{1}$ ...(1)
and $L_{2} : \frac{2x-3}{2p} = \frac{y}{-1} = \frac{z-4}{7} \Rightarrow \frac{x - \frac{3}{2}}{p} = \frac{y}{-1} = \frac{z-4}{7}$ ...(2)
If $L_{1}$ and $L_{2}$ are perpendicular to each other :
$\Rightarrow -2p + 3(-1) + (1 \times 7) = 0 \Rightarrow -2p + 4 = 0 \Rightarrow p = 2$

questions.stem: The maximum value of $Z = 4x + y$ for a L.P.P. whose feasible region is given below is :

The probability distribution of a random variable $X$ is :
X | 0 | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4
P(X) | 0.1 | $k$ | $2k$ | $k$ | 0.1
where $k$ is some unknown constant. The probability that the random variable $X$ takes the value 2 is :
questions.solution:
$\because \sum P(X) = 1$
$\Rightarrow 0.1 + k + 2k + k + 0.1 = 1$
$\Rightarrow 4k = 0.8 \Rightarrow k = 0.2$
$\therefore P(X = 2) = 2k = 2 \times 0.2 = 0.4 = \frac{4}{10} = \frac{2}{5}$

questions.stem: The function $f(x) = kx - \sin x$ is strictly increasing for
questions.solution:
Given $f(x) = kx - \sin x$
$\Rightarrow f'(x) = k - \cos x$
For strictly increasing function, we have $f'(x) > 0$
$\Rightarrow k - \cos x > 0$
$\Rightarrow \cos x < k$ or $k > \cos x$
$\because \cos x \in [-1, 1]$
$\Rightarrow k > \cos x$
$\Rightarrow k > 1$

questions.stem:
Assertion (A) : The relation $R = \{(x, y) : (x + y)$ is a prime number and $x, y \in N\}$ is not a reflexive relation.
Reason (R) : The number $2n$ is composite for all natural numbers $n$.
questions.solution:
Assertion (A) : Given relation $R$ is : $R = \{(x, y) : x + y$ is a prime number and $x, y \in N\}$
For reflexive relation, $(x, x) \in R\ \forall x \in N$
$x + x$ must be a prime number, which is not true always the case.
Hence, $R$ is not a reflexive relation. So, $A$ is true.
Reason (R) : Here, it is mentioned that the number $2n$ is composite for all natural numbers $n$, which is not always true, since $2 \times 1 = 2$ is a prime number. So, $R$ is false.
Hence, $A$ is true and $R$ is false.

options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Assertion (A) is true but Reason (R) is false.
Assertion (A) is false but Reason (R) is true.

questions.stem:
Assertion (A) : The corner points of the bounded feasible region of a L.P.P. are shown below. The maximum value of $Z = x + 2y$ occurs at infinite points.
Reason (R) : The optimal solution of a LPP having bounded feasible region must occur at corner points.
questions.solution:
Assertion (A) :
Corner Points | $Z = x + 2y$
$P(60, 0)$ | $60$
$Q(120, 0)$ | $120$ (Max)
$R(60, 30)$ | $120$ (Max)
$S(40, 20)$ | $80$
Here, the maximum value of $Z$ occurs at points $Q$ and $R$.
The maximum value of $Z$ will be obtained at infinite points on the line segment $QR$.
$A$ is true.
Reason (R) : The statement that 'The optimal (maximum or minimum) solution of a LPP having bounded feasible region must occur at corner points' is always true.
Hence, $R$ is true.
Both $A$ and $R$ are true and $R$ is not the correct explanation of $A$.

options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Assertion (A) is true but Reason (R) is false.
Assertion (A) is false but Reason (R) is true.

questions.stem: Express $\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{\cos x}{1-\sin x}\right)$, where $-\frac{\pi}{2} < x < \frac{\pi}{2}$ in the simplest form.
questions.solution:
$f(x) = \tan^{-1}\left(\frac{\cos x}{1-\sin x}\right);\ -\frac{\pi}{2} < x < \frac{\pi}{2}$
$\Rightarrow f(x) = \tan^{-1}\left[\frac{\sin\left(\frac{\pi}{2}-x\right)}{1-\cos\left(\frac{\pi}{2}-x\right)}\right] = \tan^{-1}\left[\frac{2\sin\left(\frac{\pi}{4}-\frac{x}{2}\right)\cos\left(\frac{\pi}{4}-\frac{x}{2}\right)}{2\sin^{2}\left(\frac{\pi}{4}-\frac{x}{2}\right)}\right] = \tan^{-1}\left[\cot\left(\frac{\pi}{4}-\frac{x}{2}\right)\right]$
$\therefore f(x) = \tan^{-1}\left[\tan\left(\frac{\pi}{2}-\left(\frac{\pi}{4}-\frac{x}{2}\right)\right)\right] \Rightarrow y = f(x) = \frac{\pi}{4}+\frac{x}{2}$
Aliter:
$f(x) = \tan^{-1}\left[\frac{\cos^{2}\frac{x}{2}-\sin^{2}\frac{x}{2}}{\left(\cos\frac{x}{2}-\sin\frac{x}{2}\right)^{2}}\right] = \tan^{-1}\left[\frac{\cos\frac{x}{2}+\sin\frac{x}{2}}{\cos\frac{x}{2}-\sin\frac{x}{2}}\right] = \tan^{-1}\left[\tan\left(\frac{\pi}{4}+\frac{x}{2}\right)\right] = \frac{\pi}{4}+\frac{x}{2}$

questions.stem: If $y = \cos^{3}(\sec^{2} 2t)$, find $\frac{dy}{dt}$.
questions.solution:
Given, $y = \cos^{3}(\sec^{2} 2t)$. Differentiating w.r.t. $t$:
$\Rightarrow \frac{dy}{dt} = 3\cos^{2}(\sec^{2} 2t) \times \{-\sin(\sec^{2} 2t)\} \times 2\sec 2t \times \sec 2t \cdot \tan 2t \times 2$
$= -12\cos^{2}(\sec^{2} 2t) \cdot \sin(\sec^{2} 2t) \cdot \sec^{2} 2t \cdot \tan 2t$
questions.or_stem: If $x^{y} = e^{x-y}$, prove that $\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{\log x}{(1+\log x)^{2}}$.
questions.or_solution:
Given, $x^{y} = e^{x-y}$
$\Rightarrow y\log x = (x-y)\log e$ [Taking log on both sides]
$\Rightarrow y\log x = x - y$ [$\because \log e = 1$]
$\Rightarrow y(1+\log x) = x \Rightarrow y = \frac{x}{1+\log x}$
Differentiating both sides w.r.t. $x$, we get:
$\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{(1+\log x)\cdot 1 - x\left(\frac{1}{x}\right)}{(1+\log x)^{2}}$
$\Rightarrow \frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{\log x}{(1+\log x)^{2}}$
Hence; proved

questions.stem: Find the interval in which the function $f(x) = x^{4} - 4x^{3} + 10$ is strictly decreasing.
questions.solution:
Given; $f(x) = x^{4} - 4x^{3} + 10$
$\Rightarrow f'(x) = 4x^{3} - 12x^{2} = 4x^{2}(x-3) = 0$
$\Rightarrow x = 0, 3$
when $x \in (-\infty, 0)$, $f'(x) < 0$
when $x \in (0, 3)$, $f'(x) < 0$
when $x \in (3, \infty)$, $f'(x) > 0$
so, $f(x)$ is strictly decreasing when $x \in (-\infty, 3)$

questions.stem: The volume of a cube is increasing at the rate of $6\ \mathrm{cm^{3}/s}$. How fast is the surface area of cube increasing, when the length of an edge is $8\ \mathrm{cm}$ ?
questions.solution:
Let $V$ be the volume of the cube, $S$ be its surface area and $x$ be the edge.
$\because V = x^{3}$
$\Rightarrow \frac{dV}{dt} = 3x^{2}\frac{dx}{dt}$ (diff w.r.t. $t$)
$\Rightarrow 6 = 3\times 8^{2}\times\frac{dx}{dt}$ $\left(\because \frac{dV}{dt} = 6\ \&\ x = 8\ \mathrm{cm}\right)$
$\Rightarrow \frac{dx}{dt} = \frac{6}{3\times 8\times 8} = \frac{1}{32}\ \mathrm{cm/s}$
$\because S = 6x^{2}$
$\Rightarrow \frac{dS}{dt} = 12x\frac{dx}{dt}$
$\Rightarrow \frac{dS}{dt} = 12\times 8\times\frac{1}{32} = 3\ \mathrm{cm^{2}/s}$

questions.stem: Find $\int \frac{1}{x(x^{2}-1)}\,dx$
questions.solution:
$I = \int \frac{1}{x(x^{2}-1)}\,dx$
$\Rightarrow I = \frac{1}{2}\int \frac{2x}{x^{2}(x^{2}-1)}\,dx$
Put $x^{2}-1 = t \Rightarrow 2x\,dx = dt$
$\therefore I = \frac{1}{2}\int \frac{dt}{(t+1)t} = \frac{1}{2}\int\left[\frac{1}{t}-\frac{1}{t+1}\right]dt$
$= \frac{1}{2}\left[\log|t| - \log|t+1|\right] + C$
$= \frac{1}{2}\left[\log\left|\frac{t}{t+1}\right| + C\right] = \frac{1}{2}\left[\log\left|\frac{x^{2}-1}{x^{2}}\right|\right] + C$

questions.stem: Given that $y = (\sin x)^{x}\cdot x^{\sin x} + a^{x}$, find $\frac{dy}{dx}$.
questions.solution:
Given that; $y = (\sin x)^{x}\cdot x^{\sin x} + a^{x}$
Let $(\sin x)^{x} = u$ and $x^{\sin x} = v$
$y = u\cdot v + a^{x}$
$\Rightarrow \frac{dy}{dx} = u\cdot\frac{dv}{dx} + v\cdot\frac{du}{dx} + a^{x}\cdot\log a$ .....(1)
Now; $u = (\sin x)^{x}$
$\Rightarrow \log u = x\cdot\log\sin x$ (taking log on both sides)
$\Rightarrow \frac{1}{u}\frac{du}{dx} = x\cdot\frac{1}{\sin x}\cdot\cos x + \log\sin x\cdot 1$ (diff w.r.t. $x$)
$\Rightarrow \frac{du}{dx} = (\sin x)^{x}\cdot\left[x\cot x + \log\sin x\right]$ .....(2)
and $v = x^{\sin x}$
$\Rightarrow \log v = \sin x\cdot\log x$ (taking log on both sides)
$\Rightarrow \frac{1}{v}\frac{dv}{dx} = \sin x\cdot\frac{1}{x} + \log x\cdot\cos x$ (diff w.r.t. $x$)
$\Rightarrow \frac{dv}{dx} = x^{\sin x}\left[\frac{\sin x}{x} + \log x\cdot\cos x\right]$ .....(3)
From equations (1), (2) and (3) we get;
$\frac{dy}{dx} = (\sin x)^{x}\left[x^{\sin x}\left\{\frac{\sin x}{x} + \log x\cdot\cos x\right\}\right] + x^{\sin x}\left[(\sin x)^{x}\left\{x\cot x + \log\sin x\right\}\right] + a^{x}\cdot\log a$

questions.stem: Evaluate: $\int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{4}} \frac{x\,dx}{1+\cos 2x+\sin 2x}$
questions.solution:
$I = \int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{4}} \frac{x\,dx}{1+\cos 2x+\sin 2x}$ ...(1)
$\Rightarrow I = \int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{4}} \frac{\left(\frac{\pi}{4}-x\right)dx}{1+\cos 2\left(\frac{\pi}{4}-x\right)+\sin 2\left(\frac{\pi}{4}-x\right)}$ $\left[\because \int_{0}^{a} f(x)\,dx = \int_{0}^{a} f(a-x)\,dx\right]$
or $I = \int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{4}} \frac{\left(\frac{\pi}{4}-x\right)dx}{1+\sin 2x+\cos 2x}$ ...(2)
Adding (1) and (2); we get;
$2I = \int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{4}} \frac{\frac{\pi}{4}}{1+\sin 2x+\cos 2x}\,dx$
$\Rightarrow I = \frac{\pi}{8}\int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{4}} \frac{dx}{1+\frac{2\tan x}{1+\tan^{2}x}+\frac{1-\tan^{2}x}{1+\tan^{2}x}}$
or $I = \frac{\pi}{8}\int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{4}} \frac{\sec^{2}x\,dx}{(1+\tan^{2}x)+2\tan x+(1-\tan^{2}x)}$
$\Rightarrow I = \frac{\pi}{8}\int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{4}} \frac{\sec^{2}x\,dx}{2(1+\tan x)}$
Put $1+\tan x = t \Rightarrow \sec^{2}x\,dx = dt$
When $x = 0$; $t = 1$ and $x = \frac{\pi}{4}$; $t = 2$
$\Rightarrow I = \frac{\pi}{8}\int_{1}^{2}\frac{dt}{2t} = \frac{\pi}{16}\int_{1}^{2}\frac{dt}{t} = \frac{\pi}{16}\left[\log t\right]_{1}^{2} = \frac{\pi}{16}\left[\log 2 - \log 1\right] = \frac{\pi}{16}\log 2$
questions.or_solution:
$I = \int e^{x}\left[\frac{1}{(1+x^{2})^{3/2}} + \frac{x}{\sqrt{1+x^{2}}}\right]dx$
Let $f(x) = \frac{x}{\sqrt{1+x^{2}}}$
$\Rightarrow f'(x) = \frac{\sqrt{1+x^{2}}\cdot 1 - \frac{x\cdot 2x}{2\sqrt{1+x^{2}}}}{(1+x^{2})} = \frac{(1+x^{2})-x^{2}}{(1+x^{2})^{3/2}}$
$\Rightarrow f'(x) = \frac{1}{(1+x^{2})^{3/2}}$
$\Rightarrow I = e^{x}\left(\frac{x}{\sqrt{1+x^{2}}}\right) + C$ $\left[\because \int e^{x}\left[f(x)+f'(x)\right]dx = e^{x}\cdot f(x) + C\right]$

questions.stem: Find: $\int \frac{3x+5}{\sqrt{x^{2}+2x+4}}\,dx$
questions.solution:
$I = \int \frac{3x+5}{\sqrt{x^{2}+2x+4}}\,dx$
Let $3x+5 = A(2x+2)+B$
By comparing both sides
$\Rightarrow 3 = 2A$ or $A = \frac{3}{2}$ and $2A + B = 5$
$\Rightarrow B = 5 - 2A = 5 - \left(2\times\frac{3}{2}\right)$ or $B = 2$
$\therefore 3x+5 = \frac{3}{2}(2x+2)+2$
$\Rightarrow I = \frac{3}{2}\int\frac{2x+2}{\sqrt{x^{2}+2x+4}}\,dx + 2\int\frac{dx}{\sqrt{(x^{2}+2x+1)+3}}$
$\Rightarrow I = \frac{3}{2}\int\frac{dt}{\sqrt{t}} + 2\int\frac{dx}{\sqrt{(x+1)^{2}+(\sqrt{3})^{2}}}$ [Put $t = x^{2}+2x+4 \Rightarrow dt = (2x+2)\,dx$]
$\Rightarrow I = \frac{3}{2}\times 2\sqrt{t} + 2\left[\log\left|(x+1)+\sqrt{x^{2}+2x+4}\right|\right] + C$
$\Rightarrow I = 3\sqrt{x^{2}+2x+4} + 2\left[\log\left|(x+1)+\sqrt{x^{2}+2x+4}\right|\right] + C$

questions.stem: Find the particular solution of the differential equation $\frac{dy}{dx} = y\cot 2x$, given that $y\left(\frac{\pi}{4}\right) = 2$
questions.solution:
Given differential equation is $\frac{dy}{dx} = y\cot 2x$
$\Rightarrow \frac{dy}{y} = \cot 2x\,dx$
Integrating both sides; we get:
$\int\frac{1}{y}\,dy = \int\cot 2x\,dx \Rightarrow \log|y| = \frac{\log|\sin 2x|}{2} + C$
Given that $y\left(\frac{\pi}{4}\right) = 2$
$\Rightarrow \log 2 = \frac{\log\left|\sin\frac{2\pi}{4}\right|}{2} + C$
$\Rightarrow C = \log 2$
$\therefore \log|y| = \frac{\log|\sin 2x|}{2} + \log 2$
or $y^{2} = 4\sin 2x$
questions.or_stem: Find the particular solution of the differential equation $(xe^{y/x}+y)\,dx = x\,dy$, given that $y = 1$ when $x = 1$.
questions.or_solution:
Given differential equation is: $(xe^{\frac{y}{x}}+y)\,dx = x\,dy$,
$\Rightarrow \frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{xe^{\frac{y}{x}}+y}{x}$
or $\frac{dy}{dx} = e^{\frac{y}{x}} + \frac{y}{x}$ ....(1)
Let $\frac{y}{x} = v \Rightarrow y = vx$
$\Rightarrow \frac{dy}{dx} = v + x\frac{dv}{dx}$ ....(2)
From (1) and (2);
$v + x\frac{dv}{dx} = e^{v} + v$
$\Rightarrow \frac{1}{e^{v}}\,dv = \frac{1}{x}\,dx$
Integrating both sides;
$\frac{e^{-v}}{-1} = \log x + C$
$\Rightarrow -e^{\frac{-y}{x}} = \log x + C$
Given; $y(1) = 1$
$\Rightarrow -e^{-1} = \log 1 + C$
or $C = \frac{-1}{e}$
Hence; $-e^{\frac{-y}{x}} = \log x - \frac{1}{e}$

As for the given constraints; the obtained feasible region is bounded as shown.

questions.stem: A card from a well shuffled deck of 52 playing cards is lost. From the remaining cards of the pack, a card is drawn at random and is found to be a King. Find the probability of the lost card being a King.
questions.solution:
Let $E_1$: event that lost card is a king,
$E_2$: event that lost card is not a king,
and $E$: event that the drawn card is a king.
Now, $P(E_1) = \frac{4}{52}$ and $P(E_2) = \frac{48}{52}$
Also; $P(E/E_1) = \frac{3}{51}$ and $P(E/E_2) = \frac{4}{51}$
$\Rightarrow P(E_1/E) = \frac{P(E_1)\cdot P(E/E_1)}{P(E_1)\cdot P(E/E_1) + P(E_2)\cdot P(E/E_2)}$
$= \frac{\left(\frac{4}{52}\times\frac{3}{51}\right)}{\left(\frac{4}{52}\times\frac{3}{51}\right)+\left(\frac{48}{52}\times\frac{4}{51}\right)}$
$= \frac{12}{12+(12\times 16)}$
$\Rightarrow P(E_1/E) = \frac{1}{17}$
questions.or_stem: A biased die is twice as likely to show an even number as an odd number. If such a die is thrown twice, find the probability distribution of the number of sixes. Also, find the mean of the distribution.
questions.or_solution:
Let $P(\text{even no}) = 2x$
$P(\text{odd no}) = x$
$\because P(1)+P(2)+P(3)+P(4)+P(5)+P(6) = 1$
$x+2x+x+2x+x+2x = 1$
$9x = 1 \Rightarrow x = \frac{1}{9}$
$P(\text{even no.}) = \frac{2}{9}$ and $P(\text{odd no.}) = \frac{1}{9}$
$P(2) = P(4) = P(6) = \frac{2}{9}$
$P(1) = P(3) = P(5) = \frac{1}{9}$
Let random variable $X$ = number of sixes
$X = 0, 1, 2$
All favourable outcomes for atleast one six are
$\{(1,6),(2,6),(3,6),(4,6),(5,6),(6,6),(6,1),(6,2),(6,3),(6,4),(6,5)\}$
$P(\text{atleast one six}) = P(\text{six with even no}) + P(\text{six with odd no.})$
$= 5\left(\frac{2}{9}\times\frac{2}{9}\right) + 6\left(\frac{2}{9}\times\frac{1}{9}\right) = \frac{20}{81}+\frac{12}{81} = \frac{32}{81}$
$P(X=0) = P(\text{no six}) = 1 - P(\text{at least one six}) = 1 - \frac{32}{81} = \frac{49}{81}$
$P(X=1) = P(\text{one six}) = 4\times P(\text{six with even no.}) + 6\times P(\text{six with odd no.})$
$= 4\times\left(\frac{2}{9}\times\frac{2}{9}\right) + 6\times\left(\frac{2}{9}\times\frac{1}{9}\right) = \frac{16}{81}+\frac{12}{81} = \frac{28}{81}$
$P(X=2) = P(\text{two six}) = P(6,6) = \frac{2}{9}\times\frac{2}{9} = \frac{4}{81}$
Mean $= \left(0\times\frac{49}{81}\right)+\left(1\times\frac{28}{81}\right)+\left(2\times\frac{4}{81}\right) = \frac{28}{81}+\frac{8}{81} = \frac{36}{81} = \frac{4}{9}$

questions.stem: Sketch the graph of $y = x|x|$ and hence find the area bounded by this curve, $X$-axis and the ordinates $x = -2$ and $x = 2$, using integration.
questions.solution:
Given, $y = x|x| = \begin{cases} x^{2} & ; x \geq 0 \\ -x^{2} & ; x < 0 \end{cases}$
Now, we have to find the area bounded by this curve, $X$-axis and the ordinates $x = -2$ and $x = 2$.
Now, required area $= 2\int_{0}^{2} y\,dx = 2\int_{0}^{2} x^{2}\,dx = 2\left[\frac{x^{3}}{3}\right]_{0}^{2} = 2 \times \frac{2^{3}}{3} = \frac{16}{3}$ sq. units
questions.or_stem: Using integration, find the area bounded by the ellipse $9x^{2} + 25y^{2} = 225$, the lines $x = -2$, $x = 2$, and the $X$-axis.
questions.or_solution:
Given equation of ellipse is $9x^{2} + 25y^{2} = 225$
$\Rightarrow \frac{x^{2}}{225/9} + \frac{y^{2}}{225/25} = 1 \Rightarrow \frac{x^{2}}{5^{2}} + \frac{y^{2}}{3^{2}} = 1$
Required area will be 4 times of the shaded area.
Now, $\frac{x^{2}}{25} + \frac{y^{2}}{9} = 1 \Rightarrow \frac{y^{2}}{9} = 1 - \frac{x^{2}}{25}$ or $y^{2} = \frac{9}{25}(25 - x^{2})$
Hence, required area $= 4\int_{0}^{2} y\,dx = 4 \times \frac{3}{5}\int_{0}^{2} \sqrt{25 - x^{2}}\,dx$
$= \frac{12}{5}\left[\frac{x}{2}\sqrt{25 - x^{2}} + \frac{25}{2}\sin^{-1}(x/5)\right]_{0}^{2} = \frac{12}{5 \times 2}\left[2\sqrt{21} + 25\sin^{-1}(2/5)\right]$
$= \frac{6}{5}\left[2\sqrt{21} + 25\sin^{-1}(2/5)\right]$ sq. units $= \left(\frac{12}{5}\sqrt{21} + 30\sin^{-1}\left(\frac{2}{5}\right)\right)$ sq. units

questions.stem: Let $A = R - \{5\}$ and $B = R - \{1\}$. Consider the function $f : A \rightarrow B$, defined by $f(x) = \frac{x-3}{x-5}$. Show that $f$ is one-one and onto
questions.solution:
Injectivity:
Let $x_{1}, x_{2}$ be any two elements of $A$. Then, $f(x_{1}) = f(x_{2})$
$\Rightarrow \frac{x_{1}-3}{x_{1}-5} = \frac{x_{2}-3}{x_{2}-5}$
$\Rightarrow (x_{1}-3)(x_{2}-5) = (x_{2}-3)(x_{1}-5)$
$\Rightarrow x_{1}x_{2} - 5x_{1} - 3x_{2} + 15 = x_{1}x_{2} - 5x_{2} - 3x_{1} + 15$
$\Rightarrow -2x_{1} = -2x_{2}$
$\Rightarrow x_{1} = x_{2}\ \forall\ x_{1}, x_{2} \in A$
So, $R$ is one-one or injective.
Surjectivity:
Let $y$ be an arbitrary element of $B$. Then, $f(x) = y \Rightarrow y = \frac{x-3}{x-5}$
$\Rightarrow yx - 5y = x - 3$
$\Rightarrow yx - x = 5y - 3$
$\Rightarrow x = \frac{5y-3}{y-1}$
Clearly, $x = \frac{5y-3}{y-1}$ is a real number for all $y \neq 1$.
Also, $\frac{5y-3}{y-1} \neq 5$, ($\because 3 \neq 5$)
Thus, every element $y$ in $B$ has its pre-image $x$ in $A$ given by $x = \frac{5y-3}{y-1}$
So, $f$ is onto or surjective.
Hence, $f$ is one-one onto or bijective
questions.or_stem: Check whether the relation $S$ in the set of real numbers $R$ defined by $S = \{(a, b) : \text{where } a - b + \sqrt{2} \text{ is an irrational number}\}$ is reflexive, symmetric or transitive.
questions.or_solution:
Given, $S = \{(a, b) : \text{where } a - b + \sqrt{2} \text{ is an irrational number}\}\ \forall\ a, b \in R$
(i) For reflexive relation:
Let $(a, a) \in S\ \forall\ a \in R$
$\Rightarrow a - a + \sqrt{2} = \sqrt{2}$, which is an irrational number
$\therefore$ $S$ is reflexive.
(ii) For symmetric relation:
Let $a = \sqrt{2} \in R$ and $b = 2 \in R$
If $(a, b) \in S$
$\Rightarrow a - b + \sqrt{2} = \sqrt{2} - 2 + \sqrt{2} = 2\sqrt{2} - 2$ which is an irrational number.
But $b - a + \sqrt{2} = 2 - \sqrt{2} + \sqrt{2} = 2$, which is not an irrational number $\Rightarrow (b, a) \notin S$
$\Rightarrow$ $S$ is not symmetric
(iii) For transitive relation:
Let $a = -\sqrt{2}$, $b = 3\sqrt{2}$ and $c = 2$; all $\in R$
If $(a, b) \in S$:
$\Rightarrow a - b + \sqrt{2} = -\sqrt{2} - 3\sqrt{2} + \sqrt{2} = -3\sqrt{2}$; which is an irrational number and if $(b, c) \in S$:
$\Rightarrow b - c + \sqrt{2} = 3\sqrt{2} - 2 + \sqrt{2} = 4\sqrt{2} - 2$; which is also an irrational number
But $a - c + \sqrt{2} = -\sqrt{2} - 2 + \sqrt{2} = -2$; which is not an irrational number.
$\Rightarrow (a, c) \notin S$
So, $S$ is not transitive.
Hence, $S$ is reflexive only.

questions.stem:
If $A = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 & -3 \\ 3 & 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 & -1 \end{bmatrix}$, find $A^{-1}$ and hence solve the following system of equations :
$2x + y - 3z = 13$
$3x + 2y + z = 4$
$x + 2y - z = 8$
questions.solution:
Given, $A = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 & -3 \\ 3 & 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 & -1 \end{bmatrix}$
Now, $|A| = 2(-2-2) - 1(-3-1) + (-3)(6-2) = -8 + 4 - 12 = -16 \neq 0$
$\Rightarrow A^{-1}$ exists.
Now, $C_{11} = -4$, $C_{12} = 4$, $C_{13} = 4$,
$C_{21} = -5$, $C_{22} = 1$, $C_{23} = -3$,
$C_{31} = 7$, $C_{32} = -11$, $C_{33} = 1$
Hence, $\mathrm{adj}(A) = [C_{ij}]^{T} = \begin{bmatrix} -4 & -5 & 7 \\ 4 & 1 & -11 \\ 4 & -3 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$
$\because A^{-1} = \frac{1}{|A|}\,\mathrm{adj}A$
$\therefore A^{-1} = \frac{-1}{16}\begin{bmatrix} -4 & -5 & 7 \\ 4 & 1 & -11 \\ 4 & -3 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$ ..... (1)
The system of equations is given as:
$2x + y - 3z = 13$, $3x + 2y + z = 4$, $x + 2y - z = 8$
This system of linear equations can be written as $A \cdot X = B$ gives:
$\begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 & -3 \\ 3 & 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 & -1 \end{bmatrix} \cdot \begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \\ z \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 13 \\ 4 \\ 8 \end{bmatrix}$
$\Rightarrow X = A^{-1} \cdot B$
$\Rightarrow X = \frac{-1}{16}\begin{bmatrix} -4 & -5 & 7 \\ 4 & 1 & -11 \\ 4 & -3 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \cdot \begin{bmatrix} 13 \\ 4 \\ 8 \end{bmatrix} = \frac{-1}{16}\begin{bmatrix} -52 - 20 + 56 \\ 52 + 4 - 88 \\ 52 - 12 + 8 \end{bmatrix}$ [From eq. (1)]
$\Rightarrow \begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \\ z \end{bmatrix} = -\frac{1}{16}\begin{bmatrix} -16 \\ -32 \\ 48 \end{bmatrix}$
$\Rightarrow x = 1,\ y = 2,\ z = -3$

questions.stem: Find the distance between the line $\frac{x}{2} = \frac{2y-6}{4} = \frac{1-z}{-1}$ and another line parallel to it passing through the point $(4, 0, -5)$
questions.solution:
$L_{1} : \frac{x}{2} = \frac{2y-6}{4} = \frac{1-z}{-1}$
$\Rightarrow \frac{x-0}{2} = \frac{y-3}{2} = \frac{z-1}{1}$ ..... (1)
Let $L_{2}$ be the line which passes through the point $(4, 0, -5)$ and parallel to $L_{1}$.
$\Rightarrow L_{2} : \frac{x-4}{2} = \frac{y-0}{2} = \frac{z+5}{1}$ ..... (2)
In vector form, we have:
$L_{1} : \vec{r} = (0\hat{i} + 3\hat{j} + \hat{k}) + \lambda(2\hat{i} + 2\hat{j} + \hat{k})$
and $L_{2} : \vec{r} = (4\hat{i} + 0\hat{j} - 5\hat{k}) + \mu(2\hat{i} + 2\hat{j} + \hat{k})$
Comparing them with $\vec{r} = \vec{a}_{1} + \lambda\vec{b}$ and $\vec{r} = \vec{a}_{2} + \mu\vec{b}$, we have:
$\vec{a}_{2} - \vec{a}_{1} = 4\hat{i} - 3\hat{j} - 6\hat{k}$ and $\vec{b} = 2\hat{i} + 2\hat{j} + \hat{k}$
$\Rightarrow \vec{b} \times (\vec{a}_{2} - \vec{a}_{1}) = \begin{vmatrix} \hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k} \\ 2 & 2 & 1 \\ 4 & -3 & -6 \end{vmatrix} = \hat{i}(-12+3) - \hat{j}(-12-4) + \hat{k}(-6-8) = -9\hat{i} + 16\hat{j} - 14\hat{k}$
Also, $|\vec{b}| = \sqrt{2^{2} + 2^{2} + 1^{2}} = \sqrt{9} = 3$
Hence, required distance $= \frac{|\vec{b} \times (\vec{a}_{2} - \vec{a}_{1})|}{|\vec{b}|} = \frac{|-9\hat{i} + 16\hat{j} - 14\hat{k}|}{3} = \frac{\sqrt{81 + 256 + 196}}{3} = \frac{\sqrt{533}}{3}$ units
questions.or_stem: If the lines $\frac{x-1}{-3} = \frac{y-2}{2k} = \frac{z-3}{2}$ and $\frac{x-1}{3k} = \frac{y-1}{1} = \frac{z-6}{-7}$ are perpendicular to each other, find the value of $k$ and hence write the vector equation of a line perpendicular to these two lines and passing through the point $(3, -4, 7)$.
questions.or_solution:
Given, lines $\frac{x-1}{-3} = \frac{y-2}{2k} = \frac{z-3}{2}$ ...(1)
and $\frac{x-1}{3k} = \frac{y-1}{1} = \frac{z-6}{-7}$ ...(2)
are perpendicular to each other.
$\Rightarrow ((-3) \times 3k) + (2k \times 1) + (2 \times (-7)) = 0$
$\Rightarrow -9k + 2k = 14$
$\Rightarrow -7k = 14$ or $k = -2$
Let the equation of a line perpendicular to these two lines and passing through the point $(3, -4, 7)$ be:
$\frac{x-3}{a} = \frac{y+4}{b} = \frac{z-7}{c}$ ...(3)
Now, lines (1) and (3) are perpendicular to each other.
$\Rightarrow (-3 \times a) + (2k \times b) + (2 \times c) = 0$
$\Rightarrow -3a - 4b + 2c = 0$ or $3a + 4b - 2c = 0$ ....(4) ($\because k = -2$)
Also, lines (2) and (3) are perpendicular to each other.
$\Rightarrow (3k \times a) + (1 \times b) + (-7 \times c) = 0$
$\Rightarrow -6a + b - 7c = 0$ or $6a - b + 7c = 0$ ....(5) ($\because k = -2$)
From equations (4) and (5), we have:
$\frac{a}{28-2} = \frac{b}{-12-21} = \frac{c}{-3-24} \Rightarrow \frac{a}{26} = \frac{b}{-33} = \frac{c}{-27} = \lambda$ (say)
Hence, Cartesian equation of required line is:
$\frac{x-3}{26\lambda} = \frac{y+4}{-33\lambda} = \frac{z-7}{-27\lambda}$ or $\frac{x-3}{26} = \frac{y+4}{-33} = \frac{z-7}{-27}$ [From eq. (3)]
Its vector equation is given as: $\vec{r} = (3\hat{i} - 4\hat{j} + 7\hat{k}) + \lambda(26\hat{i} - 33\hat{j} - 27\hat{k})$

questions.stem:
A store has been selling calculators at Rs. 350 each. A market survey indicates that a reduction in price ($p$) of calculator increases the number of units ($x$) sold. The relation between the price and quantity sold is given by the demand function $p = 450 - \frac{1}{2}x$.

Based on the above information, answer the following questions :
(i) Determine the number of units ($x$) that should be sold to maximise the revenue $R(x) = xp(x)$. Also, verify the result.
(ii) What rebate in price of calculator should the store give to maximise the revenue ?
questions.solution:
Given, $p = 450 - \frac{1}{2}x$
(i) $R(x) = x \cdot p(x) = x\left[450 - \frac{1}{2}x\right]$
$\Rightarrow R(x) = 450x - \frac{x^{2}}{2}$
For maxima or minima, $\frac{dR(x)}{dx} = 0 \Rightarrow 450 - \frac{2x}{2} = 0 \Rightarrow x = 450$ units
Now, $\frac{d^{2}R(x)}{dx^{2}} = -1 < 0$; when $x = 450$ units
Hence, verified
(ii) $p = 450 - \frac{1}{2}x$
At $x = 450$; $p = 450 - \frac{450}{2} =$ ₹225
The store sells calculators at ₹350 each.
Hence, the rebate in price of calculator in order to maximise the revenue is given as ₹(350 - 225) = ₹125

questions.stem:
An instructor at the astronomical centre shows three among the brightest stars in a particular constellation. Assume that the telescope is located at $O(0, 0, 0)$ and the three stars have their locations at the points $D$, $A$ and $V$ having position vectors $2\hat{i} + 3\hat{j} + 4\hat{k}$, $7\hat{i} + 5\hat{j} + 8\hat{k}$ and $-3\hat{i} + 7\hat{j} + 11\hat{k}$ respectively.

Based on the above information, answer the following questions :
(i) How far is the star $V$ from star $A$ ?
(ii) Find a unit vector in the direction of $\overrightarrow{DA}$.
(iii) Find the measure of $\angle VDA$.
OR
(iii) What is the projection of vector $\overrightarrow{DV}$ on vector $\overrightarrow{DA}$ ?
questions.solution:
Given, $\vec{d} = 2\hat{i} + 3\hat{j} + 4\hat{k}$, $\vec{a} = 7\hat{i} + 5\hat{j} + 8\hat{k}$, $\vec{v} = -3\hat{i} + 7\hat{j} + 11\hat{k}$
(i) $\overrightarrow{AV} = \vec{v} - \vec{a} = (-3\hat{i} + 7\hat{j} + 11\hat{k}) - (7\hat{i} + 5\hat{j} + 8\hat{k}) = -10\hat{i} + 2\hat{j} + 3\hat{k}$
$\Rightarrow$ Required distance $= |\overrightarrow{AV}| = \sqrt{(-10)^{2} + 2^{2} + 3^{2}} = \sqrt{113}$ units
(ii) $\overrightarrow{DA} = \vec{a} - \vec{d} = (7\hat{i} + 5\hat{j} + 8\hat{k}) - (2\hat{i} + 3\hat{j} + 4\hat{k})$
$\Rightarrow \overrightarrow{DA} = 5\hat{i} + 2\hat{j} + 4\hat{k} = \vec{r}$ (say)
$\Rightarrow \hat{r} = \frac{\vec{r}}{|\vec{r}|}$
$\Rightarrow \hat{r} = \frac{5\hat{i} + 2\hat{j} + 4\hat{k}}{\sqrt{5^{2} + 2^{2} + 4^{2}}} = \frac{5}{\sqrt{45}}\hat{i} + \frac{2}{\sqrt{45}}\hat{j} + \frac{4}{\sqrt{45}}\hat{k}$
(iii) $\cos(\angle VDA) = \frac{\overrightarrow{DV} \cdot \overrightarrow{DA}}{|\overrightarrow{DV}||\overrightarrow{DA}|}$
$= \frac{(\vec{v} - \vec{d}) \cdot [5\hat{i} + 2\hat{j} + 4\hat{k}]}{|\vec{v} - \vec{d}| \cdot \sqrt{5^{2} + 2^{2} + 4^{2}}} = \frac{[-5\hat{i} + 4\hat{j} + 7\hat{k}] \cdot [5\hat{i} + 2\hat{j} + 4\hat{k}]}{\sqrt{(-5)^{2} + 4^{2} + 7^{2}} \cdot \sqrt{5^{2} + 2^{2} + 4^{2}}}$
$\Rightarrow \cos(\angle VDA) = \frac{-25 + 8 + 28}{\sqrt{90} \cdot \sqrt{45}} = \frac{11}{45\sqrt{2}} = \frac{11\sqrt{2}}{90}$
$\Rightarrow \angle VDA = \cos^{-1}\left(\frac{11\sqrt{2}}{90}\right)$
OR
(iii) Projection of $\overrightarrow{DV}$ on $\overrightarrow{DA} = \overrightarrow{DV} \cdot \frac{\overrightarrow{DA}}{|\overrightarrow{DA}|}$
$= \frac{\overrightarrow{DV} \cdot \overrightarrow{DA}}{|\overrightarrow{DA}|} = \frac{[-5\hat{i} + 4\hat{j} + 7\hat{k}] \cdot [5\hat{i} + 2\hat{j} + 4\hat{k}]}{\sqrt{5^{2} + 2^{2} + 4^{2}}}$
$= \frac{-25 + 8 + 28}{\sqrt{45}} = \frac{11}{\sqrt{45}}$ units

questions.stem:
Rohit, Jaspreet and Alia appeared for an interview for three vacancies in the same post. The probability of Rohit's selection is $\frac{1}{5}$, Jaspreet's selection is $\frac{1}{3}$ and Alia's selection is $\frac{1}{4}$. The event of selection is independent of each other.

Based on the above information, answer the following questions :
(i) What is the probability that at least one of them is selected ?
(ii) Find $P(G \mid \overline{H})$ where $G$ is the event of Jaspreet's selection and $\overline{H}$ denotes the event that Rohit is not selected.
(iii) Find the probability that exactly one of them is selected.
OR
(iii) Find the probability that exactly two of them are selected.
questions.solution:
Let $R$, $J$ and $A$ be the events of selection of Rohit, Jaspreet and Alia respectively; for three vacancies in the same post.
These events are independent of each other (given)
Also, $P(R) = \frac{1}{5}$, $P(J) = \frac{1}{3}$ and $P(A) = \frac{1}{4}$
$\Rightarrow P(\overline{R}) = \frac{4}{5}$, $P(\overline{J}) = \frac{2}{3}$ and $P(\overline{A}) = \frac{3}{4}$
(i) $P(\text{at least one of them is selected}) = 1 - P(\text{none of them is selected}) = 1 - P(\overline{R} \cap \overline{J} \cap \overline{A})$
$= 1 - P(\overline{R}) \cdot P(\overline{J}) \cdot P(\overline{A}) = 1 - \left(\frac{4}{5} \times \frac{2}{3} \times \frac{3}{4}\right) = 1 - \frac{2}{5} = \frac{3}{5}$
(ii) If $G$ is the event of Jaspreet's selection and $\overline{H}$ denotes the event that Rohit is not selected; then $P(G \mid \overline{H}) = \frac{P(G \cap \overline{H})}{P(\overline{H})} = \frac{P(G) \times P(\overline{H})}{P(\overline{H})} = P(G) = \frac{1}{3}$
(iii) $P(\text{exactly one of them is selected}) = P(R \cap \overline{J} \cap \overline{A}) + P(\overline{R} \cap J \cap \overline{A}) + P(\overline{R} \cap \overline{J} \cap A)$
$= \left(\frac{1}{5} \times \frac{2}{3} \times \frac{3}{4}\right) + \left(\frac{4}{5} \times \frac{1}{3} \times \frac{3}{4}\right) + \left(\frac{4}{5} \times \frac{2}{3} \times \frac{1}{4}\right)$
$= \left(\frac{1}{10} + \frac{1}{5} + \frac{2}{15}\right) = \frac{3 + 6 + 4}{30} = \frac{13}{30}$
OR
$P(\text{exactly two of them are selected}) = P(R \cap J \cap \overline{A}) + P(\overline{R} \cap J \cap A) + P(R \cap \overline{J} \cap A)$
$= \left(\frac{1}{5} \times \frac{1}{3} \times \frac{3}{4}\right) + \left(\frac{4}{5} \times \frac{1}{3} \times \frac{1}{4}\right) + \left(\frac{1}{5} \times \frac{2}{3} \times \frac{1}{4}\right)$
$= \left(\frac{1}{20} + \frac{1}{15} + \frac{1}{30}\right) = \frac{3 + 4 + 2}{60} = \frac{9}{60}$
